Leaving them, she went forth into the sky seeking food such as grass seeds and the fruits of the *aśvattha* tree; after wandering among the forests and returning again and again, she remained there, guarding those eggs.
Then, in that nest thick with the body-feathers of the female pigeon and warmed by the heat generated from the pressure of her limbs,
the young pigeons, their bodies pale-red, broke through their eggs and emerged.
Then, beholding those fledglings whose tips of their beaks were repeatedly opened by hunger, she,
disregarding her own great hunger, nourished them with priyaṅgu and nīvāra fruits.
Seeing their mother holding the seed, those young pigeons,
with the tips of their wings quivering, repeatedly spread out their faces and uttered plaintive cries.
Then, at the conclusion of his meditation, that sage— his senses stilled and desiring to go to the edge of the forest for the sake of gathering fruit—
saw a female dove carrying grass, wood, and fruit, and stood still as she settled upon his head where a nest was located.
Then the Bodhisattva thought: "It is certain that this female dove has given birth here within the mass of my matted hair, which serves as a nest constructed from bits of grass and wood.
If I were to rise and go to gather fuel, roots, tubers, and fruits, then it is certain that this poor creature would come to this place."
Today, no longer seeing these young pigeons with their copper-colored palates revealed,
it will repeatedly fly up into the sky from its perch in the trees and circle about in grief.
Alas! This latent impression from the delusions of hundreds of births persists, since even among animals there is such a deeply rooted denial regarding their own offspring.
If there were neither offspring nor friends nor even kinsmen, one would be one's own protector; since there is no other protector, and being without seed, how could there be any denial?
When there is no denial [of reality], mental afflictions do not cloud the mind;
when mental afflictions are absent, one who is free from attachment dwells in happiness, endowed with tranquility.
Deluded by afflictions, people conceive the notion that offspring are to be produced;
thus the foolish person falls into exhaustion, tormented by remorse.
Just as a cow, even though unwilling, is yoked by force by a powerful cart-driver,
so too is this person of evil intellect cast into the ocean of existence by their own karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
Therefore, as long as these young pigeons have not yet fledged while remaining in the hollow of my matted hair,
I shall remain here with an immovable form, my mind and body satisfied by the nourishment of the nectar of meditation.

Having reflected thus, out of compassion for the young pigeons and disregarding his own hunger, the Bodhisattva again assumed the cross-legged posture and gladdened himself with the bliss of meditative concentration.

When the young pigeons had fully developed their wings and flown up into the sky together with their mother, a deity dwelling near that place approached, beheld the Bodhisattva, and with a mind overcome by wonder, exclaimed: "Oh, this Great-souled One!"
Out of compassion for living beings, the great seer arose from his previous meditation and, in order to protect the dove, once again rendered himself motionless through meditation and remained thus.
"And this Great-Souled One will not remove this pigeon-nest from his head even when these young pigeons have departed;
therefore, I myself shall remove this abode of pigeons fashioned upon his crown of matted locks. Having thus reflected, he [acted].
With her two hands, as tender as young shoots, she very slowly removed from the head of that best of sages the nest that was scattered here and there with fragments of eggs.
When that deity had departed, the Bodhisattva withdrew his mind from meditative absorption, and perceiving the lightness of his head, he reflected as follows:
When the young pigeons, whose wings had fully developed, had gone to the edge of the forest with their mother,
my dwelling was surely removed from my head by someone deeply inclined toward devotion.
Having reflected thus, that Great-souled One rose, brought sacrificial wood, kuśa grass, flowers, and fruits, and performed his ritual ablutions.
Having offered oblations into the fire whose flickering flames blazed at midday, and having consumed the fragrant fruit that was free from all impurity,
he sat beneath a tree with his eyes fixed on the tip of his nose and, with a single-pointed mind, began once more to practice yoga.
Thus, having perceived reality through meditative absorption, although that Blessed One was capable of entering nirvana while still in the state of a bodhisattva,
he wandered throughout saṃsāra— which is full of many calamities— for the sake of the welfare of the world; reflecting on this, one should generate supreme faith in the Buddha, the Blessed One.
// The Jājvali-jātaka, the sixth // ...
32. Wise men protect even a blade of grass with the greatest effort if it has been entrusted to them by another.
How much more so those who are wearyless in casting themselves for the sake of sentient beings, being heavy with wisdom?
As it is heard:

[of that mountain] whose clouds were shattered by striking against its snowy peaks that resembled pillars of polished silver; where the tracks of yaks’ hooves were followed by flocks of hunters upon the snowfields white as heaps of pearl-dust; whose various hollows were made uneven by the scraping of the horns of Śiva’s bull; and whose thickets were dark with groves of many *bhūrja*, *sarala*, *devadāru*, *nameru*, and *padmaka* trees.

In some places, the ground at the roots of the trees was washed by the waters of spreading waterfalls; in others, because of the great medicinal herbs (*mahauṣadhi*) blazing during the night, it was as if illuminated by thousands of lamps;
in others, the interior of the vine-bowers on the shores of Lake Mānasa was made fragrant by the enjoyments of Vidyādhara couples;
and in some places, the grass was uprooted by the stamping of the feet of startled antelopes (*nyaṅku*), which had been struck down by blows from the tips of *kesari* flowers.

[It was] a place where the dark soil of the meadows was marked by the red lac from the soles of Umā’s feet; elsewhere, its inner groves were strewn with the ripe fruits of trees broken by the beaks of birds;
fragrant with the scent of various flowers spread abroad by the wind; where the buds and sprouts of the trees had begun to swell at the onset of the month of Madhu;

where the waters of the Gaṅgā’s bank were abandoned by flocks of birds terrified by the cries of ospreys; and where herds of deer stood motionless, listening to the songs of playful pairs of Kinnaras.

In a certain region of the Himālaya mountain, which had attained a height like that of the Ocean of Milk due to its lofty peaks, there stood a cave of no great size; its stone floor at the entrance was respectfully honored with offerings of flowers by the trees,
its borders were darkened by the sprouting of young green grass-blades, and its vicinity was adorned by a pond filled with blooming lotuses.
Dwelling in a cave, his neck was encircled by filaments as tawny as fine silk threads sprinkled with an abundance of thick turmeric water;

his tongue was exceedingly tremulous and delicate like a young sprout; his body was pale as a heap of slightly withered *atimuktaka* flowers; his fangs were sharp and curved like the tip of a crescent moon; he possessed a broad chest, stout forearms, and a slender waist; and his pair of eyes was tawny like glowing embers of khadira wood.

Once there was a Bodhisattva, a lord of beasts named Aninditāṅga (Blameless Limb), whose curved claws were like the beaks of hawks, whose tail-hair was dark at the tips, who was like an ornament of the Snowy Mountain, and who never terrified elephants or deer. Then, perceiving his natural goodness— like that of a sage whose mind is benevolent toward all living beings— [he was honored].
Naturally auspicious and with lovely eyes, the deer followed him joyfully, as if he were their kinsman.
Endowed with tranquility, clad in the bark of *kesara* trees, followed by deer,
that ascetic who was a lion among men slowly emerged from the interior of Guha’s hut and ate the ripe fruits of the trees.
Wandering within the forest for the sake of enjoying its fruits, he— moving with playful grace and possessing beautiful, swaying filaments—
was awaited by the trees like a guest by great householders who are fond of hospitality.
As he emerged from the interior of the cave at the end of winter, the sun, appearing like a lotus opening wide with its excessive yawn,
gradually spread before him a new warmth as a gift, providing comfort to his limbs.
"This lord of beasts upon this mountain is like Tārkṣya, the bird of great prowess among winged creatures"—
as if out of such agitation at his presence, the Night held up the moon as a parasol over him.
Standing on the bank of that river whose waters were as clear as the moon and cool, he drank;
and she, as if considering herself to have fulfilled her purpose, clearly seemed to laugh with her rows of foam.
The Himalaya mountain was inhabited by that great-souled lion of pure mind;
he considered himself even more joyful than the Golden Mountain (Meru), as he shone exceedingly with his own greatness.
"How can there be a nature that strikes terror into the world, and how can there be such great compassion for deer?
Thinking thus, even the enemies of deer bowed down to that lord of beasts as he stood upon the Himalayas like a sage.

Then once, as that lord of beasts sat before the mouth of a cave— which was as delightful as a king’s pleasure garden, charming with the lute-like sounds of swarms of bees being struck by the sprout-fingers of nearby dancing flowering creepers, and where peacock dances were set in motion by the drum-like resonance of spreading waterfalls— a certain creature appeared. Its face was as crimson as a mass of pressed lac-dye, its eyes matched the fresh *āmalaka* fruit, and it held two ripe *udumbara* fruits.
Having bowed down to the pair of monkeys, whose shoulders were occupied by two disciples and whose fingers were soiled and moist with the juice of fruit, he said:
"Oh, how irreproachable is the deed of your speech, body, and mind!
That you are called 'Aninditāṅga' (One of Irreproachable Limbs) is remembered as being truly consistent with your character."
Oh! Your qualities—renunciation, patience, vigor, profundity, compassion, and the rest—O best among the virtuous, surpass even the sages. (HJm 32.11)
"Aha! By your pure conduct, you whose mind is pure, even the hearts of the cruel have been brought to the highest state of gentleness."
"Blessed is this blessed Himavat, with its rocky surfaces covered in snow"—
it was with such a resolute nature that you took refuge in it.
"Therefore, having entrusted these two children— who are terrified at the sight of fierce beasts— to you, we two shall go to the forest seeking fruit."
"Until we have returned from the depths of the forest with our fruit,
you must protect these two, whose limbs are so unsteady."
This pair—monkey-like fickleness and instability—is simultaneous;
therefore, you must endure for a moment the affliction caused by these two.
Even the most grievous sufferings, the wise endure for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others, having no regard for their own happiness.
How will he who desires to utterly rob those of timid hearts of their fear not endure the tormenting pain that distresses the mind? (HJm 32.18)

Thus addressed by that pair of monkeys for the sake of protecting their daughter, the lion—though capable of guarding others like a king—fell into a moment of agitation and reflected as follows: HJm_32.19 //
"For even a great heap of gold can be guarded when placed under the charge of another;
how then can these two monkey-children, who are by nature fickle, be protected?
Or rather, how could I—who must protect the entire world from the fear of cyclic existence—not protect these two?"
"However, it is not right for me to deliberate upon this," the Great Being decided, and having resolved thus, he spoke to that pair of monkeys:
"Go, plunge into this Snowy Mountain which, with its lofty peaks, seems to scrape the very center of the sky;
bring back sweet fruits as quickly as possible, while I lovingly care for these two young ones."
Then that pair of monkeys, having left their two young ones near the Bodhisattva and comforted them, hurried away through the depths of the Himalayan forests to gather fruit.
While those two monkeys were gone, the two young apes felt a bond of affection for that great-souled lion as if for a father.
And Aninditāṅga gave them fruits that were sweet when ripe, which they held with the tips of their loosened teeth.
And because of their natural fickleness, those two repeatedly committed various acts of harassment against that Great Being.

While Hari, desiring sleep, lay in a charming forest grove at the edge of a cave where a pleasant, cool breeze blew, those two young monkeys repeatedly destroyed his happiness of momentary slumber with their clamor. (HJM 32.21)
When his eyes were slightly closed by sleep,
he pricked them with two fingers, their pupils reddened like sparks of fire.
While he sat there comfortably,
they stood nearby and, seizing his tail at its tip, repeatedly pulled it back and forth with great force.
Grasping his mane and repeatedly mounting his back,
they flew up again and again from their natural restlessness, leaping high into the air and then falling back down.
Even though abundant fruits were present before them, the two of them plucked a fruit from the mouth of that hungry man.
Thus, because his heart was auspicious with compassion, he endured those various misdeeds of the two young monkeys as if they were those of his own sons.
The minds of the virtuous— who are equanimous toward all things, indifferent to pleasure and pain, and capable of bearing every burden— never experience weariness.

Then once, a vulture named Kṣuraka— possessing a mass of exceedingly harsh and broad wings, with curved and rough claws, naturally fierce eyes, a beak as sharp as a whetted razor, and having failed to find any flesh for food— suddenly swooped down with a loud rush from the expanse of the sky toward those two who were near the Bodhisattva, drawn by the scent of the fruit.

The two young monkeys, their rows of white little teeth chattering, their distorted faces wide with fear, and uttering most piteous cries, were seized by the feet; then, leaping swiftly into the air, they vanished upon the peak of the Snowy Mountain.
The Bodhisattva, however, crying out, "Alas! Alas! thought: "If I attack this vulture with my prowess, he will fly up again and hide on another, even more inaccessible, peak."
This pair of young monkeys would surely perish;
by no means can I bear to look upon this pair of monkey infants,
whose eyes are agitated by increasing agony and whose cavities of the palate are marked by piteous cries.
Its feathers wet with blood flowing from its belly, its flesh being torn away by a hungry hawk.

Now that the flesh has been torn away by this vulture, and these two young monkeys have approached him with fruits to their heart's content, what shall I be able to say to them today in their presence?

Have those two fickle ones gone to drink the water of the lake, or have they climbed a tree for the sake of fruit and settled there? Or have they entered this mountain cave, or perhaps been destroyed here by some serpent? (HJm 32.30)
"O Lord of Beasts, why do you stand silent with your face cast down? Tell me, where could these two young ones have gone?
How shall I hear such words from those two monkeys, their eyes so piteous and their speech faltering with distress?

After a long time, perceiving the absence of those two sons whose rows of teeth were as white as jasmine buds, they will approach them in grief and perform the funeral rites for them, like the trembling of fish pulled out by a hook.

Therefore, I think this is the opportune moment here: before this vulture, tearing open their bellies with a beak shaped like the tip of a tiger’s claw, pulls out the entrails of us two trembling monkeys, I shall go to the edge of a peak on the Himalayas and, having settled there facing upward, I will lead him to a state of righteousness through conciliation and skillful means.
Having reflected thus, that Great-souled One approached the vulture and said:

"O best of birds, these two fledglings were entrusted to my hands by their parents; therefore, it is not right for you to destroy them while they have their mouths gaping with hunger and their cries are piteous.
Surely, you too must once have had children of your own."
Whatever kind of affection you have for them, such is the affection of others as well.
Thus, taking compassion as your guide, do not kill these two young monkeys;
for even by eating them while they are still alive, you will find no ultimate satisfaction.
Fie, alas, on the life of that person, and fie on such self-love, who nourishes the impurity of this wretched body by harming others! (HJm 32.36)
From ignorance arises attachment even toward this body which is full of defects;
through that, the ignorant person performs actions that serve as the cause for miserable rebirths in order to nourish it.
For one who perceives everything as empty due to the absence of self and what belongs to the self,
the darkness arising from unreal conceptualization does not obstruct the mind.
When the wise one attains reality through the absence of darkness,
he then turns away from both the auspicious and the inauspicious for the sake of liberation.
It is clear on this earth that there is no other flesh-eater more cruel than a lion;
yet, even though I have entered this miserable lion womb, I do not desire this unrighteous injury to living beings.

O best of birds, wandering through the sky, you shall see a deer here in this dense forest frequented by the king of beasts, either struck down by its enemy or dead of its own accord; having approached it with swift motion, you shall eat its flesh.
Therefore, even if you endure a great hunger that sears the body like a flame of fire, do not, having abandoned negligence, commit such an unwholesome act that leads to falling into hell. HJm_32.42.

The fires of hell, described by the wise as terrifying with the *huṃ* sounds produced by the cracking of internal bones and joints, spreading a mass of sparks and fearsome with their broad, red, and smoky crests; these masses of flickering flames cause anguish to people even when merely heard of, let alone when touched.

Beholding even a man depicted in a painted mural, being cooked in a hellish cauldron made of iron— its surface heated by the touch of a blazing fire, its interior filled with boiling, swirling oil, and its neck and mouth emitting a deep roar while his eyes are squinted shut— who, even if naturally fierce, would not desist from cruelty, the cause for reaching such miserable states?
He who, having heard of the sufferings of the miserable realms, does not desist from unwholesome deeds,
is either a man in name only or one whose heart is like stone.
Then that vulture, his mind purified by the Bodhisattva’s teaching of the Dharma, bowed down and said:
"Lord of beasts, you have explained this characteristic of the fool;
you should now explain the characteristic of the wise man."
Then the Bodhisattva, perceiving that his mind was serene, said to him:
"If it is so, then hear the characteristics of a wise man:
whether in loss or in gain, toward a friend who speaks for one's welfare or toward an enemy, in praise or in blame, or in great prosperity or in calamity."
He who, established with a mind purified by tranquility, does not undergo transformation, stands above the wise like the sun among luminous bodies.
Or rather, what is the use of hearing these definitions of a wise man from you?
Let these two young monkeys be released; I shall give myself to you.
Eat my flesh, drink my blood, and pluck out my eyes while I remain motionless.
Having spoken thus, he remained for a long time with his eyes closed and his body motionless.
Then the drum situated in the midst of the Lord of the Gods' city resounded, filling the quarters with its sound;
and the Siddhas, stationed in the sky, praised the lion with their heads bowed, having offered their bodies to the vulture.
The earth, with its golden mountains shaken, trembled; the host of the thirty gods, together with Indra, was struck with wonder;
and showers of flowers were rained down upon him by the lords of serpents who had offered hymns of praise.
Then the bird placed the two young monkeys near the lion’s cave;
their bodies were torn by his claws, they were motionless, and their eyes were closed due to the fainting fit caused by fear.
Having approached the Bodhisattva slowly, that best of vultures raised him up; standing before him with a humble disposition, he spoke this kind of praise with devotion: HJm_32.51 //

Where is this compassion of yours, O exalted one, and where is this lionhood that strikes fear into the world? For some extraordinary reason, you have long been a certain sage acting like a lord of beasts.
He whose mind relies on wisdom and remains equanimous in both suffering and happiness is the one who,
at the cost of his own life, rescues another fallen into calamity.
If virtuous bridges such as you were not steadfast,
living beings would sink into the bottomless and vast ocean of suffering.
Having heard this auspicious teaching of the Dharma from you,
from this day forward I shall practice compassion even toward my enemies.
"And I ask you further: what station do you desire by means of this asceticism?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"It is struck by a succession of sufferings arising from the exhaustion and affliction caused by wandering through beginningless saṃsāra."
This is my earnest effort for the sake of delivering the world from the ocean of existence and for the attainment of the state of a Tathāgata.
The vulture said: For one such as you, possessed of great wisdom, the state of a Buddha is by no means difficult to attain—

[you who are] profound and unassailable, discerners of existence and non-existence, whose intellects have been revealed through the scriptures of action, and whose souls are devoted to the task of benefiting others.
May our association with those like you—who understand the words of the Tathāgatas that destroy existence and are the virtuous ones who dispel delusion—occur in birth after birth.
I have placed two young monkeys there near the cave;
therefore, O virtuous one, you ought now to let me depart.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Aha! You possess sharp discernment, since you have grasped this instruction of mine.
He who does not grasp even a gross thing when it is made clear by the words of a kinsman will find his mind laboring in vain regarding the subtle subject matter of the treatises."
How can one who has developed cataracts perceive a minute hole at the door of his house, even when it is illuminated, if he lacks the power to see it?
Even when an instructor is present, a fool who is negligent does not abandon his perverse intellect;
though repeatedly brought to straightness, a dog's tail returns once more to its curvature.
With his mind directed downward by the clear scriptures that have shown him the path, he does not go astray;
like a lordly elephant with a sharp and auspicious mind, his body surrounded by clever bamboo-carrying attendants.
This collection of senses, when well-restrained, produces no transformation in the wise man;
for a serpent with its hood firmly grasped is not able to cause even the slightest harm.
The profound harm one inflicts upon a wicked person spreads the fruit of that injury far and wide;
it is like yellow arsenic poured into the mouth of a snake, which turns its venom even more virulent.
Desire, having first been conquered by the enemies that are the senses through negligence, casts people into misfortune;
like a flame that appears beautiful with its molten gold, it hurls the heedless moth into the fire.
Attachment to the objects of the senses causes an unwise person to fall from the path of his own duty,
just as the ripening of fruit causes it to fall from the top of a tree when its root at the base is obstructed by loose bonds.
If poisonous trees, venomous serpents, weapons, and fire did not exist by their very nature as oppressors, with what else could the wicked person of turbid and sharp mind be compared? HJm 32.66.

One who is prone to groundless anger, harsh in speech, wicked, with eyes made crooked by a frown, and like an anthill from which many terrifying serpents emerge through various openings, inspires excessive fear. (HJm 32.67)

Whom does the wicked man, devoid of shame, not torment when he comes within range with the sharp edge of his speech-sword, which is whetted upon the stone of anger and raised joyfully for the purpose of striking down others? (HJm 32.68)
Wicked men, bearing the armor of deceit, difficult to restrain for long while stationed in the midst of the army of the senses,
heartless and wounding even toward virtuous people, let fall their words like the edge of a sword upon the earth.

A wise person should not place trust in a wicked person, even if that person is dressed modestly, speaks pleasantly, possesses a handsome body, and has a melodious voice; does not the peacock, despite its beautiful form and lovely cry, devour hissing serpents?
If you desire to nourish the family of the mind for a long time, or to increase the queen of wisdom,
then, upon the rising of the cloud of insight, let the seed of excellent qualities be sown within yourself.
A self-possessed man whose mind has long been purified by association with the virtuous never falls into the company of the wicked;
a bee that frequents the lovely blue lotus flower never settles upon a corpse.
Just as delight arises in an archer who has reached the battlefield and whose arrows have not missed their mark,
so it is for the wise man who has struck down the enemy of the defects with the arrows of his virtues that fall even from afar.
Having obtained this most pure, unassailable, and natural ornament of virtues, honored by noble beings,
a person no longer feels wonder even at the ornaments of the best of gods.
Seeking ultimate happiness or the arising of virtuous qualities,
one should therefore abandon wicked people and rely upon a spiritual friend.
The company of ignoble people never brings joy to a virtuous person,
just as a garment that has been washed with waters from sacred fords does not become stained by anything other than white.
Through association with the wise, who dispel darkness and destroy the evils of the world, even a cruel person abandons their foul nature and adopts goodness.
For that very water which a person, parched by thirst, does not wish to drink when it is in the ocean, instantly loses its saltiness once it has entered the belly of a rain cloud.
"Go then as you please," said the Bodhisattva; and having circumambulated that Great Being,
the bird flew up into the expanse of the sky and, while circling about, beheld a tiger devouring his flesh— the tiger whose claws, mouth, and whiskers were stained red with blood,

whose shoulders were thick with accumulated fat, whose interior of the mouth was made fragrant by the taste of fresh *mustā* grass, and whose pair of curved fangs were soiled by tossing them upon the surface of the earth.
He beheld a young boar whose body was slightly smeared with mud, surrounded by a circle of vultures not far away, and watched by a flock of noisy crows perched in the trees nearby.

Seeing this, he thought: "As long as this tiger, having finished his meal, goes to his own dwelling, I shall remain in a secluded spot. Having waited there in due course, when the tiger had become satiated, had obtained his fill, and had returned to his own abode at his leisure, [the lion approached].
Having consumed a pala of boar meat, even the hawk, though his fat was bound [by the meal], quickly returned to his own nest.
Even the lord of beasts, while the sun— red as a crest of *kiṃśuka* flowers— remained upon the summit of the golden mountain with its radiant rays,
returned to his own dwelling, his soft mane-tip stirred by the fluttering birds nestled in the thickets of the tree branches.

And having seen those two young monkeys—their bodies torn by thorns and claws, their movements stilled, and their eyes closed under the power of a swoon—he felt his heart ache with sorrow. Thinking, "May there be relief for them through a sprinkling of water; I shall dispel their fainting," he observed that the water was obstructed by trees whose roots were like coral sprouts and which clung to the bank without any gaps.
Slowly approaching with a heart longing for the lotus, she plunged into the lake whose filaments were tawny with pollen.
Having plunged into that great lake and swiftly emerged,
he whose mane was hanging down approached the vicinity of the cave, repeatedly bending the young grass by the placement of his hooves.
Then, over those two young monkeys whose bodies were wounded by the claws of the cold vultures,
the lion swiftly shook his mane, from which water trickled down.
Being sprinkled with water from the mane of Harikesara, the two young monkeys regained consciousness as their heavy fainting fit passed;
with their mouths wide open and quivering, they opened their eyes.
Terrified by the vulture and trembling with fear, the two of them approached the feet of the lord of beasts and stood there;
then he too, with affection, repeatedly licked them with his tongue, which was as beautiful as a swaying sprout.
Having eaten a ripe fruit fallen from its stalk, and having consoled it again and again with affection as if it were his own child,
he entered his cave, which flickered like a glowworm lamp, and embraced the two of them, sleeping happily through the night.

Gradually, as the western quarter was being abandoned by the moon, which had grown pale from its crown of withered mālatī flowers; as the sprouts of grass were being nibbled by the deer that had just risen from their dwellings; as the waters of the ocean were being colored by the morning twilight;

as the host of stars was becoming sparse; as the pools of water were becoming exceedingly beautiful through the awakening of the lotus groves; and as the interiors of the forests were rendered more enchanting by the crests of peacocks moving as they descended from the branches of the trees.
When the night had passed, he of blameless deeds and faultless limbs was, as it were, being reverently sung to by swarms of bees moving among the flowers at the edges of the shrubs near the cave;
while the sun, like a vessel of refined gold, was ascending toward the quarter of Indra.
Accompanied by young monkeys and with his hanging mane quivering, he slowly emerged.
Then, having taken the fruit, the couple of monkeys, eager with joy to see their two sons who were greedy for fruit,
quickly arrived at the dwelling of the lord of beasts.

To that couple who had approached him—having abandoned pride, arrogance, and elation; speaking softly with gentle words and filled with compassion—the Lord Hari, the knower of the world, having first received their salutation, addressed them with words of auspiciousness.
Then, he related to the two young monkeys everything that had happened in due order, and finally, he told them of their abduction by the vulture.
Then, having heard that their two sons had passed away,
the two monkeys, out of grief, touched the limbs of the pair that were mangled by vultures.
And they both spoke these very tender words of praise to the lord of beasts:
"While you protect our two sons, we too are well protected."
Spreading the Ganges of Dharma-discourse, marked by the mountain peaks of your virtues,
and shrouded in the snow of your fame, you are a moving Himalaya.
Since your innumerable virtues cannot be contained within your body,
I believe they have assumed the form of filaments and remained outside.
The lord of birds agitates the still waters of the ocean as he flies; the radiance of the moon does not spread when it is shrouded by masses of clouds.
But your mind, established in that state which cuts through all evil, is pure and cannot be led to alteration, for it is no longer susceptible to the influence of passion and ignorance.
"By the great merit you have acquired through protecting these two sons of ours, may you obtain the desired fruit."
Therefore, having taken these two little sons under your care, may you protect them with diligence until they reach their own dwelling in the depths of the forest, a place surrounded by many kinsmen.
Having been told by him, "Go," and having offered their salutations with devotion to that holy man, the two of them,
eager and mounted on the backs of young elephants, departed very slowly from that peaceful place toward the edge of the forest.
Once their parents had departed, the two of them, mounted upon the middle of their backs and clinging firmly to the mass of hair on the necks,
turned their eyes back with longing and gazed again and again at the king of beasts.
Having entrusted that deposit— the essence of all deposits— within the range of his essential wisdom,
he experienced even greater joy, like one who has set down a burden from his shoulder upon the ground, thereby cutting off his weariness.
There is nothing more difficult for living beings than the entrusting and holding of a deposit,
nor is there any other happiness for humans than its restitution.
Thus, reflecting that even while existing in the animal realm, the Blessed One protected the deposit of living beings for a very long time,
and that even in such a state he cultivated wisdom—
how excellent was the deposit of the Dharma made by that Protector!
It must be strictly observed by you who desire ultimate happiness.
Thus ends the Siṃhajātaka. ...
35. Great-souled ones, desiring the welfare of the three worlds, renounce even divine happiness, O Śākyasiṃha.
For the suffering of others weighs more heavily upon the hearts of the compassionate than their own suffering.
Thus it is heard: having attained all the perfections and being close to enlightenment, the Bodhisattva—his limbs illuminated by his own radiance—was once born in the Tuṣita heaven.
That Great Being, having revealed the true path to the gods dwelling there through a discourse on the Dharma, reflected as follows:
"In the Kṛtayuga, indeed, the world, being devoted to righteousness, was easily led onto the path of truth.

But in this Kaliyuga, living beings are overcome by intoxication, pride, greed, passion, hatred, and delusion; their minds are deluded by a mere fragment of pleasure, and they are headed for miserable rebirths.
Therefore, it is fitting that I, having realized enlightenment, should rescue the world from cyclic existence."
And in the Middle Country, the people possess minds purified by faith;
furthermore, this King Śuddhodana in the great city of Kapilavastu surpasses even the great ṛṣis by his exceedingly virtuous conduct.
Therefore, thinking, "I shall take birth from the womb of Māyā, his chief queen," he appeared in a dream while she was sleeping at night.
Having assumed the form of an elephant, white as the Himalayan mountain, with six great tusks and a face perfumed by the scent of ichor,
he entered the womb of the queen of King Śuddhodana for the sake of destroying the world's suffering.
Then Queen Mahāmāyā reported that dream to the king:
"O King, in my dream today, it is said, a lordly elephant with six tusks, white as an autumn cloud, broke through my right side and entered my womb.
Thereupon, the king described that dream in the presence of the twice-born who were experts in interpreting the results of dreams.
And those brahmins said to him,
"Great King, a universal monarch (cakravartin) shall be born as your son.
With a joyful mind, the king honored those twice-born ones and dismissed them.
Then, at one time, the queen, accompanied by the women of the inner apartments and having experienced the most excellent longings, went to Lumbinī with the king’s permission.
As the goddess was leaning against a branch laden with the weight of flowers,
the Bodhisattva quickly emerged, splitting open her womb.
Then, as soon as he was born, the thousand-eyed Indra, fair as a golden pillar, joyfully and gently took him up;
and from the sky, showers of māndārava flowers fell upon his head along with two pure streams of water.

Established by the Destroyer of Māra as the sole lord of the world, the steadfast one gradually took seven steps upon the earth and uttered these most wonderful and peaceful words: "This is my final birth, for there is no longer any darkness within me."
Then his radiance, which eclipsed the brilliance of the cool-rayed moon and illuminated the earth,
pierced through the darkness in the hells of terrifying gloom— a darkness impenetrable by the blazing rays of the sun and the moon.
"Here is the Great-Souled One, the King of Dharma, who has been consecrated!"—thus, with hearts full of joy, the immortals struck their drums in the vault of the sky.
And the Queen, having ascended the palanquin and taken the Bodhisattva with her, went to her own palace.
Then Śuddhodana, his mind filled with wonder at this most marvelous event, ordered the release of all prisoners and had the streets and marketplaces adorned with raised banners and flags.

The king caused the city of Kapilavastu to be adorned such that its ground was sprinkled with most fragrant scented water, and the spaces between its streets were variegated with offerings of fresh flowers. From the sky,

the lord of the earth heard from the people a report descending upon him like a mass of fire-flames— a mass of matted locks whose shoulders were covered with the skins of dappled deer, which bore the accumulation of both dark and non-dark deeds.

Then the king, rising up, approached the great seer who had learned of the Bodhisattva’s birth as he was entering; having greeted him and honored him with the offering of water for the feet and other marks of respect, and after the seer had accepted a seat and been asked about his welfare, the king showed him the Bodhisattva resting in the nurse's lap and said:
"Blessed One, let this son of mine first be seen; will he be long-lived?"
Then Asita, having gazed upon the Bodhisattva, thought thus:
"Since he is adorned with these distinct marks as if with ornaments,
he will likewise become a Buddha for the sake of removing the suffering of the world."
When he has become a Buddha, I shall then pass away;
those embodied beings who hear from me this discourse on the Dharma are truly fortunate.
As that great seer of pure mind was reflecting thus,
his eyes, with the tips of their lashes bent down, became filled with tears.
Then Śuddhodana, beholding Asita with tearful eyes, spoke in agitation: "Surely this one is short-lived;
for that reason the Blessed One has come to have tearful eyes."
"Alas! This lotus of my son, not yet in bloom, will be uprooted by the lordly elephant of Death.
Asita replied, "Enough, enough, Great King; do not grieve."
"I grieve for myself because,

when he has abandoned these sense-objects and, having beheld embodied beings seized by old age and death, goes with a distressed mind to the forest of asceticism to become a Buddha, then I shall meet my death; therefore, out of grief for me, this [tear] has come with tears."
After that great seer had departed, saying, "The eye has been restored," they gave the Bodhisattva the name Siddhārtha.
Then, after a short time, having acquired all branches of knowledge from his teacher, he chose a bride named Yaśodharā from a family of equal status and brought her home as his wife.

Thinking, "How might this son of mine remain ignorant of old age, death, and disease? Śuddhodana caused the Bodhisattva to remain within the inner apartments of the palace, devoted exclusively to the uninterrupted sight and sound of dance and song. And having fathered a son named Rāhula by Yaśodharā, he once [visited] pleasure groves adorned with songs.
Having heard this and resolved to go forth, he was granted permission by his father; mounting his excellent chariot, he traveled about, beholding the streets of Kapilavastu adorned with splendor.
Then, having heard from his attendants that he was delightful to the eyes, like the god of love himself, with long ears and wide eyes—
Various activities arose among the women of the city, their minds intensely eager for the sight of him.
Then, a certain woman, whose forehead was adorned with a fresh tilaka mark from her unfinished decoration, and whose one eye was anointed with kuvalaya paste that had slipped from her ear,
pointed out the prince— who resembled the god of love— as he was departing, saying to her friend, "Look at him," while holding a paint-stick in her lotus-like hand.
Another, thinking, "Oh, how fortunate is Yaśodharā, who is his partner in the practice of Dharma," gazed upon him for a long time with fixed eyes.
Yet another shone intensely like a stone statue supporting the window-pillars with both hands;
[another asked: "Why are you walking so very hurriedly out of curiosity to see the prince?"

"Pick this necklace back up; it is only half-fastened and is falling from the slope of your breast! Thus speaking, "Oh, how restless you are! the elders look on in anger. "Why are you so shameless? one woman reproached another.
Yet another, by the touch of her heavy breasts against a portion of the door, seemed as if she were granting it permission to open halfway.

"Do not let your curiosity to see the prince be satisfied by you alone; grant me this interval as well, for I too am curious and desire to see the prince. Thus she spoke. As those women, desiring to see the prince, spread out, the sound of their girdles and anklets resounded throughout the mansions.
Then, as the prince proceeded along the road, he beheld in due course an old man whose trembling hand rested upon a staff,
whose splendor had departed, whose head was exceedingly white, who appeared as if fashioned from pure funeral ashes, and whose body was bent low.

Then the Bodhisattva asked the charioteer, "Tell me, who is this man with his bow strung, his limbs bent and frail, his hair as white as the blossoms of the kāśa flower, who is seen looking about as if lamenting with a shaking of his head?
The charioteer replied:

"Prince, that which is called old age pervades the entire world; it robs the body and the senses of their vigor, and like an enraged woman toward young men, it dispels the intoxication of youth, by which this man has been brought to such a state. Then that Great-souled One spoke again:
"If old age thus destroys youth, what delight indeed can there be in this perishable body?
Sūta said:
"O Prince, it is not only old age; disease as well, arising from the disturbance of the bodily constituents (dhātus), is a great misfortune for embodied beings."
Beyond that is death, known as the one most skilled at stripping away all activity and the greatest of calamities, which produces great suffering for embodied beings even when merely contemplated.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Alas! This world is daily pursued by these three enemies: death, disease, and old age."
When there exists such great and terrible fear, how can this world remain solely devoted to sense objects?
"O charioteer, turn back the chariot quickly; go home again. Why linger here?
For me, who am apprehensive of death, disease, and old age, there can be no delight in this grove."

Then the king, having heard that the Bodhisattva was distressed in mind and recollecting those words of Asita, his heart filled with the apprehension of a future separation from his son, commanded the charioteer:
"The prince must be taken to the pleasure grove.
And that charioteer, having forcibly brought him into the very grove, spoke to him.

The Venerable One ought to behold here something of these young vine-maidens of the grove, who possess a beauty made manifest by the smiles of their blossoms; as they are slowly, slowly made to dance by the Malaya breeze creeping along,
there shine upon them at their edges the curved braids of swarms of bees buzzing and wandering about.
Then the Bodhisattva, descending from his chariot, his mind agitated by reflections on old age, death, and disease, spoke like a lordly elephant pierced by an internal barb:
"These things that cut through the fortitude of the weak-minded, which end in bitterness and are avoided by those of tranquil soul like fierce serpents— "
Even for a youth devoted to the god of love, the objects of the senses do not distract his mind, for it is the world that is his rival.

Then that king dispatched beautiful women skilled in dance and song to that grove in order to captivate the heart of the Bodhisattva. Having approached the prince, they displayed various gestures, emboldened by the intoxication of passion. Then one among them said to him, "Behold, O Prince!"
These fragrant Malaya breezes blow, shaking the flowering trees; the bee circles the blossoming cluster of the mango tree;
and the cuckoo, with its loud cry, seems to urge on the Flower-Arrowed God, who holds this long string for his bow’s drawing—yet you remain at ease! I fear he will provoke him.
Moreover:
"The slender maiden, her limbs anointed with saffron and wearing a cluster of mango blossoms as a garland, seems for a moment to be eclipsed by a noble bee as it hovers about her. (HJm 35.20)
Another, however, said this to him:
"Beholding the bees— the attendants of the creepers who have enjoyed her— dusty with the pollen of those flowers, the lotus-pond,
with its young lotuses shaken by the breeze, seems to threaten them again and again."
But one woman said to him:
"I am going for your sake to gather these flowers that are densely packed with subtle nectar;
meanwhile, O Prince, ward off from afar the bee whose restless flight obstructs my vision."
Another, standing near him with a smile, addressed him:
"Having placed upon your chest a flowery bow, white as a conch-shell fragment, its string made of *bakula* fibers and its filaments shaken by bees,
Love— certainly closing one eye— is straightening his flower-arrow, desiring to strike you who treat him with contempt due to your profound composure."
The Bodhisattva said:
"Enough, enough, sisters, with these idle prattle!
Indeed, in my agitated mind, erotic discourses can find no place now, just as streams of water find no place in a fire."
Having heard those words of his, "Sisters," the women lowered their faces in shame, casting aside their playful coquetry.
Perceiving that group of young women to be abashed and the prince of pure intellect to be agitated,
Smara— having surely placed his flowery arrows in the quiver— lowered his bow with modesty.
Then the Bodhisattva, finding no pleasure there in the grove of dalliance, mounted his excellent chariot as the sun was setting, and those women returned to the palace.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva, disregarding talk of amorous passion, lay down upon his couch; fixing his mind solely upon old age, death, and disease, he became absorbed in reflection.
Then, in order to stir that Great Being to spiritual urgency, the Śuddhāvāsa deities immediately induced sleep in the attendants guarding the bed.
And there, some had faces with teeth revealed by the force of incessant gasping breaths, their edges covered by trickling streams of saliva;

while others lay like the bodies of the dead upon the paved floor, their silk garments loosened and slipping away so that their thighs were exposed, their pearl necklaces scattered over their breasts, and their vine-like arms tossed about in disorder.
And another, with her face resting upon a pillow formed by her two arms folded over a *muraja* drum, fell from her seat and lay there as a student;

in the hand of yet another, the flute—its first hole separated from the lip and dark as the pupils of a woman’s eyes—fell away because sleep had loosened the grip of her fingers. Beholding their various states, like lotus-stalks churned by elephants, the staff-lamps seemed to laugh.
Then the Bodhisattva, having censured those young women, rose up and went out; he raised up Chandaka and said:
"Intent on crossing over this ocean of existence, I am prepared to go to the forest of asceticism.
Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing my resolve, bring the horse Kanthaka, who possesses great speed."

And Chandaka, though urged by those pure-dwelling deities, disregarded that royal command; having assented with "So be it," he brought forth Kanthaka, the noble horse, with a sword fastened to his left flank.

Then, at the break of dawn, the young yakṣas caused the Bodhisattva, mounted upon that horse with Chandaka trailing behind holding the reins, to descend through the sky near the hermitage of the great seer Arāḍa, their hooves resting upon the palms of their hands.
Then, having removed from his body the ornaments that were radiant with the brilliance of clear gems,
he slowly cut with his sword his wavy hair, which was as dark as the throat of a cuckoo.
Beholding him bereft of ornaments like a clear pool of water from which the lotuses have been removed, Chandaka,
tormented by the fierce fire of grief, shed drops of tears from his eyes that resembled pearls.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Indeed, a virtuous person ought not to feel despondency when a friend or a kinsman, intent upon the Dharma, has set out for the forest of asceticism. Therefore, go and speak thus to my elders."
"Or else, this body of mine shall waste away through intense austerity,
or I shall attain that state which has been seen by those who perceive reality."

Chandaka, having replied "So be it" to the Bodhisattva, bowed before him and took the horse and the ornaments; proceeding by stages, he arrived at the city and reported the Bodhisattva’s message to the King.
Upon hearing his resolve, Śuddhodana, together with the women of the inner apartments, lamented in many ways.

And the Bodhisattva, having purchased two saffron-colored robes from a son of the gods who had assumed the form of a hunter—using a pair of garments as bright as moonbeams—and having put them on, proceeded slowly toward the hermitage of Arāḍa.
He went there.
And seeing the Bodhisattva approaching, Arāḍa said, "Welcome, welcome! Having led him into his own hut and seated him upon a cane chair, he engaged him in conversation concerning matters of welfare.
Then the Bodhisattva questioned him.
"What is your Dharma like, or how is it realized?
O most excellent of beings, you ought to tell the truth to me, who am desirous of seeing it."
Arāḍa said:
"O highly fortunate one, you ought to hear this:
birth, old age, and death are declared to be the true nature of both the primary elements and their transformations."
Nature consists of the five great elements, the ego-sense, and the manifest;

and the modifications consist of the sense organs, their objects, the hands, feet, speech, anus, genitals, and the mind— one who understands this field is designated as the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña).
Those who know reality describe the self as the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).
Furthermore, that which has birth and end, and whose nature is subject to death, should be understood as the manifest (*vyakta*); the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is the opposite of this.
Ignorance, action, and craving are to be known as the causes of saṃsāra.
A living being situated within this triad does not exist apart from the state of *sattva*.

[The afflictions are: misconception (*vipratyaya*), egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), doubt (*saṃdeha*), deluge (*abhisaṃplava*), lack of distinction (*aviśeṣa*), lack of means (*anupāya*), attachment (*saṅga*), and falling away (*abhyavapāta*).
Misconception (*vipratyaya*) is defined as functioning in a perverted manner.
The notion "I speak," "I know," and so forth, is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).
However, he who perceives even unambiguous entities as a single unity, like a lump of clay, should be considered one possessed of doubt (*saṃdeha*).
And that which is "I" is precisely those very things: the mind, the intellect, and the activities.
They declare that the merging [of the self] consists in the thought, "I am this group.
Furthermore, the lack of distinction between the awakened and the unawakened, as well as the lack of discernment regarding the *prakṛtis*, is to be understood as "non-distinction.
Indeed, it should be understood that the utterances of *svāhā* and *vaṣaṭ*, sprinkling with water, pouring over with water, and so forth, are not the means [to liberation].
When a person of little intelligence develops attachment toward an object through mind, speech, intellect, and action, that is called *abhiṣvaṅga*.
That suffering which one conceives of as "this is mine" or "I belong to this" is *abhyavapāta*.
Indolence (*ālasya*) is the cause of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) for living beings.
Darkness (tamas) and delusion (moha) are death and birth;
great delusion (mahāmoha) is designated as desire (kāma);
and let it be understood that gloom (tāmisra) is anger (krodha).
Despair, moreover, is designated as *andhatāmisra*.
Bound in mind by this fivefold ignorance, the fool repeatedly returns to the great suffering of birth and so forth.
Therein, perceiving himself as "I am the seer, the hearer, the thinker, and the agent and the instrument," he wanders about in *saṃsāra*.
And by these reasons, the flow of the stream of birth is observed; from the absence of causes comes the absence of birth.
In this regard, one who desires liberation should understand both the awakened and the unawakened, as well as the manifest and the unmanifest.
Having comprehended this fourfold set, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), liberated from all suffering, attains the imperishable state.
Having first abandoned the bond of worldly existence and its primary seed, and having taken up the ascetic marks while desiring the happiness of liberation,
one who possesses contentment and seeks the unsurpassed state should dwell at the edge of the forest, having embraced pure ethical discipline.

Thereafter, having understood that danger arises from passion and security from dispassion, he restrains the entire collection of sense-faculties, relies upon the tranquility of the mind, and thereby attains the first dhyāna— which is secluded from sensual desires and secluded from ill-will and the like, born of seclusion, and accompanied by vitarka. Endowed with such tranquility, which censures desire and hatred, he reaches the Brahma-world.
Having recognized those discursive thoughts as disturbers of the mind, he attains the second dhyāna, which is free from them and consists of the nature of joy and bliss (*prītisukha*).
With his mind being carried away by that joy, he is reborn among the Ābhāsvara gods.
Furthermore, he who withdraws his mind from that joy and bliss attains the third dhyāna, which is devoid of joy and bliss.
With his mind immersed in that third dhyāna, he obtains birth among the Śubhakṛtsna gods.
Having attained such bliss, he who maintains equanimity toward it attains the fourth dhyāna, which is free from both pleasure and pain.
And because of the length of its lifespan, some consider that very state to be liberation itself.
Why? Because of the cessation of pleasure and pain and because the mind is free from activity.
Wise men declare that the fruit of this meditative absorption (dhyāna) is common with that of the Bṛhatphala deities.
And having emerged from that samādhi, observing the defects of embodied beings, he attains knowledge for the sake of the cessation of the body.
Furthermore, having abandoned even that meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), desiring further distinction, he becomes detached even from form (*rūpa*).
First, observing with his intellect those sufferings that exist within this body, he then generates an inclination toward space (*ākāśa*) even regarding solid substances.
Having contracted the self (*ātman*) as it resides in space and beholding infinite space, through the attainment of distinction and through skill regarding the self—

Having withdrawn the self into the self, having attained the designation "nothingness" by thinking "there is nothing at all," and being liberated through the separation from the body, he is called "released.
The Bodhisattva said:
If the volitional agent truly exists, how will there be liberation?
For as long as that exists, wholesome and unwholesome actions continue to proceed.

Just as a seed is not seen to sprout by anyone in the absence of water and soil, yet is seen to sprout through those very conditions, so too should the self be understood. Furthermore, liberation is determined to result from the abandonment of karma, ignorance, and craving; yet, if a self exists, we do not perceive such abandonment. And since there is no abandonment of these without abandoning the self, how can there be liberation? Moreover, if a self exists, how could the abandonment of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) ever occur?

Having declared, "As long as there is egoism, this stream of births remains indeed," that one of great intelligence departed from that hermitage of Arāḍa and withered his body through difficult and intense austerities.
Realizing that "enlightenment to the truth does not come through this asceticism," the Bodhisattva, his body exceedingly weak, rose up,
bathed in the river Nairañjanā, and having consumed the alms-food offered by Sunandā, he was praised at the proper time by the king of serpents.
His body was encircled by a row of blue-jays with long blue wings and pale pink limbs.
With a garland of lotuses whose petals were trembling, as if interwoven with the leaves of blue water-lilies.
Then, having gone to the seat of enlightenment, the wise one, possessing the luster of a golden mountain, sat beneath the Bodhi tree for the sake of awakening.
Then, taking up a bow made of flowers, she came together with her daughters,
born of the mind, in order to disturb his heart.
Smelling a fresh *mālatī* flower before him,
one woman closed her eyes, while another closed her gaze with its tremulous pupils.
Whispering something into her friend’s ear with a slight smile,
that graceful lady Līlāvatī departed, revealing her face.
Another, her desire fulfilled, showed the bull among Jinas the garment that had slipped from the hips of Rāmā, its girdle loosened.
Where is this moon-like youth of yours, and where is your mind’s desire for asceticism?
Indulge in passion; therefore, turn back from it. Tell me, what fruit is there for you to obtain through penance?
Out of a desire for your welfare, I speak to you: what more than this do you wish to attain?
Is there any other merit that exists apart from the great dharma of a householder, which does not obstruct [the path]?
"O wise one, why is she so unfeeling toward these captivating women who are eager for your favor?"—
thus speaking with a smile on her face, the loving woman scratched the lotus-like faces of her suitors with her fingernails.

And when the Bodhisattva remained with eyes as motionless as those in meditative absorption—even while those women cast about their poisonous glances with disdain and displayed various gestures—then Māra commanded:
"Terrify him and make him rise!
Thereupon, a certain lion-faced being hissed again and again.
For the sake of terrifying the Bodhisattva, he scattered sparks from a fire.
Those sparks of fire, released from the mouth of that servant,
fell upon the sage and in an instant turned into blossoming flowers.
When he, with his hundred mouths, hurled a sharp-pointed spear,
it became a crest of blue lotuses with a mass of blooming filaments.
By another, who had fangs and was as tawny as lightning,
hot iron balls were hurled, which in an instant became flowers.
The arm, raised by another tawny-eyed man with a sword,
which was as tall as a pillar of red iron, became motionless in an instant.

Then, by the wind of the perfected mantra of the Conqueror of Mada, the host of servants carrying fire on the shore of the ocean was driven from all sides by the companion of the dark-pathed one (the wind); like a hundred stars whose luster has faded, they were scattered in distress.
Then, when the God of Love was despondent because his army had been shattered, the Blessed One arose from the fourth dhyāna and reflected thus:
"If merit and demerit were produced for oneself solely from pleasure and pain,
how could there ever be goodness among embodied beings, and how could there be an absence of dharma?"
How is the distinction between physical beauty, fortune, and so forth accepted here, if there is no prior action?
If there is no prior action, how can there be good and evil in this world?
If action were the cause of actions, then [the world] would not conceive of essence and so forth;
if the world were without cause, who would speak of the ownership of one's own actions? (HJm 35.51)
If pleasure were the cause of pleasure, and suffering the cause of suffering,
then how could liberation come about through such difficult asceticism?
Some who are ignorant declare that Īśvara is the cause;
for how could there be no equality in the world, since he is the one who dwells equally within all?
Thus, some who are ignorant and proponents of existence and non-existence,
being deficient due to their evil views and karma, are even born in the hells.
Through the karma of right view, auspicious and proclaiming noble wisdom,
some have gone to the heavenly world by means of restraint of body, speech, and mind.
Alas! The world is devoted to existence and is afflicted by the multitude of defilements;
ruined by old age and disease, it dies and is born again.
Then this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "When what exists do aging and death come to be, and by what condition?
Again, this thought occurred to him:

That is to say: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; with birth as condition...
Thus arise aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; such is the origin of this entire great mass of suffering.

From the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness; from the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form.

From the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases; from the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact; from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; from the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; from the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; from the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; and from the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair cease.
"Thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
In this way, the eye of wisdom arose for the Bodhisattva;
then that Blessed One, the Buddha, became the illuminator of the light of wisdom.
Having risen into the air, he let out a lion’s roar.
I am a lion among the creatures that are disputants; free from passion and without outflows, devoid of egoism, I shall bring an end to the suffering of sentient beings.
Then the earth, together with its mountains, trembled; the ocean surged, overstepping its shores;
and the drums of the gods, resonating with a deep and gentle sound, thundered forth.
The quarters of the sky shone with clear ornaments, and the sun and moon gleamed like those of autumn;
scented flowers, colored with swirling sandalwood powder, fell from the heavens.
The gods, accompanied by hosts of Apsarases, arrived there with eyes blossoming in wonder;
a breeze of delightful quality blew, and joy expanded within the minds of all living beings.
Uttered by great hosts of beings whose minds were filled with joy and who were struck with wonder,
auspicious words concerning the praise of the Buddha’s preeminent qualities were heard on all sides.

Oh, what magnanimity! Oh, what excellent wisdom! Behold the purity of this mind! Oh, the total detachment of his intellect from its own pleasures! Homage be to you, whose fortitude and prowess are so utterly marvelous! (HJm 35.63)
The world has truly attained a protector through you, who possess the splendor of a fully blossomed lotus-eye;
indeed, the accumulations of merit have at last become fruitful in form, for by means of Dharma, victory has been mightily won after a long time.
And all the Buddhas, speaking to the Buddha, exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!
and they presented golden jeweled parasols to Suśrī.

Then all the hosts of gods, perceiving the Bodhisattva seated at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), having attained the superknowledges (abhijñā), having conquered the forces of Māra, with his victory-banner, flags, and pennants raised high, the physician among men, the lion free from fear, the well-tamed elephant, who had attained the three knowledges (traividyā), possessed the prowess of the ten powers (daśabala), and had realized awakening through his former vows, paid him full honor and made this request:
O Lord, steadfast one, slayer of Māra, bull among Jinas, today,
while the world has thus become blind, shine forth the lamp of wisdom!
Upon this world afflicted by hunger and thirst, whose intentions are impaired by wrong views,
let the nectar of the Dharma rain down from the clouds of all the perfections.

Thus, all the hosts of gods, being satisfied, stood right there with palms joined in reverence. Then, the beautiful-faced deities of the desire realm performed his fruitful consecration with fragrant flowers, parched grain, parched rice, and water, using golden jars accompanied by song and instrumental music.
Then the Tathāgata Mahānanda, thinking, "I shall teach the Dharma to all sentient beings," rose up and set out to wander.
Then Māra approached the Blessed One and said:
"May the Buddha enter final nirvāṇa, he who is free from mental constructs and volitions."
For the great sages, being wise, have indeed attained nirvāṇa through their vows.
When Māra had spoken thus, the Blessed One said to him:
"O Evil One, I shall not enter into final nirvāṇa for the time being."
Monks, as long as there are not wise, self-controlled, learned,
and confident monks who have attained the awakening of noble knowledge and are deeply versed in the scriptures.
As long as the Three Jewels have not become renowned in the world,
Bodhisattvas who have conquered their desires are unable [to fulfill their aims] through the perfection of generosity and the other [perfections].
"O most evil one, as long as I have not attained enlightenment and conquered my enemies, I shall not go to nirvāṇa, nor shall I bring about the end of existence."
When the Lord of the Śākyas had spoken thus, the Flower-Armed One (Kusumāyudha) hung his head and,
feeling as if he were struck by a wooden club, despaired while scratching the earth.
Then the daughters of Māra, seeing their father filled with despair, approached him suddenly and addressed him:
"Why are you dejected, dear father? Tell us, if that man can be bound with the noose of passion, we shall bring him here like an elephant."
"And having quickly brought him here, I shall bring him under your control.
Father, do not fall into despair; what fear can there be from this man? (HJm 35.76)
Māra said:
"That Sugata is an Arhat in the world; he would not fall under the power of passion.
He has transcended my domain; therefore, I grieve most bitterly."

Then, out of feminine fickleness and unaware of the Bodhisattva’s power, those women— intoxicated by their abundant youth— hearing the command of their father, approached the Bodhisattva and set about to disturb his mind.
An irreproachable woman, graceful and speaking sweetly, addressed that lord of the Śākyas:
Displaying her breasts which surpassed the frontal lobes of an elephant, she, smiling, [displayed] her face as the moon and a lotus.
Sovereignty over the world under a single umbrella, fresh youth, and a lovely, gentle form—
having abandoned all these, for what purpose do you delight in asceticism, O you whose body is so desirable to me?
Another woman, Surāmā, whose eyes were like those of a young fawn and whose limbs were unsteady from intoxication, slowly approached him;
surpassing both a royal elephant and a swan in her gait, she smiled slightly and then spoke to the sage.
"O King, I wear these ornaments of gold and pearls upon my body solely for your sake;
enjoy at will the fruit of your asceticism, for even sages wander about when they are attached to sensual desire."
Having covered half her face with a cloth and fixed her gaze upon the banner of the sage lineage,
she stood before him, gracefully unfolding a lotus as if to say something indescribable.

"If you have compassion for the world, yet intend to leave behind your mother, father, and friends to dwell in the forest—whom then will you rescue? Such was the bold challenge that seemed to arise within her mind.
In whatever ways those playful women endeavored to overcome the sage with their charms,
he of the steady, long eyes remained just as motionless, free from desire and devoid of ego.
Displaying their inner states to the sage, yet unable to steal his mind,
they approached him with bodies deformed by old age and shrouded in darkness due to the offense against his ascetic power.
Then, having gone into the presence of their father, they spoke thus:
"Father, you speak the truth to us; he is not being led away by passion.
We grieve that he has transcended our domain."
"Therefore, Father, it would be well for you to make this body, worn out by old age, disappear. Māra said:
'I do not see any man in this world, including its moving and unmoving beings, who would be able to alter the Buddha’s empowerment.'"
Go quickly to him and pray to that ocean of virtues;
he will restore your bodies to their former state according to your wish.
Then, having made their request to the Tathāgata, they returned to their own abodes with bodies more beautiful than before, having regained their former splendor.

Now, when a storm arose, the Naga King Mucilinda emerged from his own abode and, thinking, "May the Blessed One not suffer from the cold," covered the body of the Blessed One with seven hoods. When the storm had passed, he prostrated to the Tathāgata and went to his own abode.
Then the Carakas, Parivrājakas, Vṛddhaśrāvakas, Gautamas, Nirgranthas, Ājīvikas, and others, having prostrated before the Tathāgata who was staying at the foot of the Nyagrodha tree, said:
"Has this seven-day storm been spent properly and happily by the Blessed One Gautama?
The Blessed One replied:
There is happiness for one who is content in solitude and always established in peace;
there is happiness from detachment in this world through the complete transcendence of evils.
Then the Tathāgata, experiencing the bliss of meditative concentration, remained at the foot of the Tārāyaṇa tree.

At that very moment, the two merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika, taking various goods and traveling from the southern region toward the northern region, beheld the Tathāgata—his body serene and clothed in saffron robes—and were filled with great joy; they bowed their heads at his feet.
They presented him with alms-bowls filled with honey and milk-rice.

Then, knowing it was the time for the Tathāgata’s meal, the four Great Kings, together with their retinues, performed worship with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, musical instruments, cymbals, and songs, and offered him bowls of clarified butter.
Then the Blessed One, having accepted those bowls, spoke to them with auspicious words:
"May prosperity be in your right hand; may prosperity abide in your left hand.
May prosperity be yours in all worlds, like a garland resting upon your head."
May the gods grant you well-being as you stand or travel upon the road;
may your mind always be set on dharma, and never at any time on evil.
May you always attain your goals, be free from disease, and enjoy a supreme lifespan;
through this deed, may you become followers of the Buddha, sons of the Sugata.
Having heard these words of the sage, which illuminate the lotus of the mind,
they went for eternal refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Then this thought occurred to the Tathāgata:
"This awakening has been attained by me through great hardship in the ultimate sense;
yet if I were to teach it to others and they did not understand it, that would be of no use."
Having thus resolved, the sage, who knew the essence of things, became silent;
for one situated in the midst of fools shines with the splendor of a brahmin through his silence.

Then, indeed, the brahmin Śikhin, impelled by the rays of the Tathāgata, together with the hosts of gods headed by Śakra, illuminated the night with a divine radiance; and having paid homage to the Tathāgata, he entreated him for the teaching of the Dharma:
"O Blessed One, kindle the lamp of wisdom in this world blinded by delusion!"
Upon this world afflicted by hunger and thirst, rain down the nectar of the Dharma!
For if you were to attain awakening only through such ascetic hardships,
then this world would go to its destruction, being mired in the pleasures of meditative absorption.
Then the Tathāgata assented to that brahmin Śikhin by remaining silent.
At that very moment, due to the evil conduct of the people of Magadha, a great portent arose.
Once again, the brahmin Śikhin addressed the Tathāgata in this way:
O Blessed One, in the land of Magadha, the world has become distressed by great portents; people are impaired and afflicted by spirits and yakṣas.
Rain down the nectar of Dharma to extinguish the fire of their sins;
now, make your former vow bear fruit.

Then the Blessed One, surveying that entire world-system with his Buddha-eye, saw the worldly condition of the low, the high, and the middling; and reflecting on whether or not he should teach, being impelled by compassion, he accepted the request of the brahmin Śikhin to teach the Dharma,
thinking, "I shall teach the Dharma."
Then the brahmin Śikhin, his mind filled with joy, paid homage at the feet of the Sage and departed for his own home.
Thereupon, the deity of the Bodhi tree bowed and spoke thus:
"Lord, where will you turn the wheel of Dharma?"
The Tathāgata said:
"In Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park. Why?
Because Kāśī is a meritorious land, well-supplied with food, and a refuge for virtuous people.
Where the gods always dwell, though they are immortal, they desire death.
Moreover:
"The wheel set in motion there by the previous Tathāgatas, Buddhas, future ones as well shall turn right there, the wheel of Dharma."
Then, seeing the Tathāgata setting out with the intention, "I shall go to Vārāṇasī," an Ājīvaka paid him homage.
After exchanging various greetings and pleasantries with him, he inquired about the Blessed One’s purpose for traveling, and the Tathāgata said to him:
"I shall go to Vārāṇasī; having gone there, I shall turn the wheel of Dharma in the city of the yogins."
For the world that has become blind, I shall fully illuminate the torch of the Dharma.
"Go, Gautama! Having been thus addressed, that Ājīvika rose and departed facing toward the south.

The Tathāgata, likewise proceeding toward Vārāṇasī, crossed the great river Gaṅgā through the air; traveling by stages on a tour of the countryside, he took up his bowl and robe and entered the great city of Vārāṇasī for alms.

Having wandered for alms there and finished his meal, he sat cross-legged upon a jeweled lion-throne prepared by the deities in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, remaining with his body stilled in meditative absorption.
Then the five monks of the auspicious group, having bowed their heads at the feet of the Tathāgata, sat down with palms joined in reverence.
Thereupon, a ray of light issued from the body of the Tathāgata, illuminating the entire world-system and inspiring them.

Having attained this human birth, which is difficult to find, the perfection of the opportune moment is extremely rare; and the appearance of a Tathāgata is as exceedingly rare as the blooming of the udumbara flower.
"Today the Buddha has gone to Kāśī for the sake of pacifying the suffering of the worlds;
therefore, you must apply your minds to the Dharma, having arrived here with all haste."
Then, from all directions, hosts of bodhisattvas endowed with their former vows,

world-protectors such as Śakra and Brahmā, and gods, asuras, yakṣas, gandharvas, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, nāga kings, and humans, having come from their respective abodes, performed a great worship of the Tathāgata and prostrated at his feet.
They stood right there, facing the Blessed One.

Then the bodhisattva named Dharmacakrapravartana circumambulated the Blessed One, prostrated, and offered a thousand-spoked wheel made of all kinds of jewels, adorned with garlands of various fragrant flowers, for the purpose of worshipping the Tathāgata.
With palms joined in reverence, he entreated him to set the Wheel of Dharma in motion:
"O Blessed One, tiger among sages, conqueror of Māra, bull among Jinas, blow the conch of Dharma to terrify the deer-like followers of false paths! (HJm 35.105)
"You who previously made a vow with [the words] 'from the east' and so forth:
'May I become a Buddha in the worlds for the sake of pacifying the suffering of sentient beings.'"
Therefore, O Blessed One, O Protector, fulfill your vow;
otherwise, the Blessed One would not be the Teacher for a world agitated by the suffering of existence.
Through your devotion to Dīpaṃkara, you have now become a Buddha;
seeing the world ablaze with the fire of suffering, shower down the nectar of immortality!
Brahmā and the other world-protectors have assembled, desiring to hear [you];
turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of abandoning the root of suffering.
Then the Great Buddha, the Lion of the Śākyas, an ocean of compassion, spoke after looking upon the assembly and addressing the group of five monks.
The sprout of the aggregates grows, produced from the seed of ignorance;
having drunk the sap of merit and demerit, the great tree of existence comes to be.
Its fruit is great and sweet, yet its ripening turns into poison;
knowing it thus to be a poisonous fruit, the wise should abandon it from afar.
To burn the sprout of the poison-tree, let the seed itself be consumed;
once the seed of ignorance is burnt, liberation will certainly be yours.
Thus the Blessed One, the Buddha, the charioteer who subdues men,
having set the wheel of Dharma in motion, then further taught the Dharma.
For the disciples, it is the Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path,
the holy life that is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end.
Then, as if from great joy, the earth with its mountains and forests trembled, its garment of the oceans held still;
the sound of celestial drums spread through the sky, and the quarters of the world shone, adorned with clarity.
Clouds that were laughing with frequent, gentle thundering and girded with lightning on all sides,
scattered showers of flowers upon him incessantly, as pollen was dispersed by their mutual collisions.
Carrying along the fragrant pollen born of the flowers of various trees, the wind, moving with a steady course,
joyfully honored him as if with unseparated, devout, and fine silken garments.
Then, throughout the entire realm, all became practitioners of the holy life;
having heard the Buddha’s words, they were devoted solely to the Buddha’s Dharma.
Then they all rose up, performed worship to the Teacher of the World,
and saying, "Today the world shall have its protector," they departed with joy.
The Blessed One, too, having resolved, "I shall effect the deliverance of all sentient beings," set out upon a journey through the countryside.
Thus, this Blessed One, desiring the welfare of the three worlds, abandoned even divine bliss and performed what is difficult to do; therefore, one should cultivate supreme faith in the Buddha.
And one should listen to his Dharma with reverence, thinking, "In this way he attained awakening through such hardships."
This prince, though satisfied with the pleasures of sovereignty, having desisted from the enjoyment of celestial women and having abandoned all royal luxuries like a blade of grass,
became pained by the suffering of others; practicing austerities difficult to perform, he conquered the powerful Māra and, having attained perfect enlightenment, became a Buddha.
"This very Blessed One, the Lion of the Śākyas, is the Lord of the three worlds"—thinking thus, a person seeking awakening must renounce even the pleasures of sovereignty;
one must undergo hardships and must conquer Māra as well. Thus, a Bodhisattva must possess the longing for awakening.
Thus ends the Jātaka of the Tathāgata Śākyasiṃha.
